questions.title: Design an ETL pipeline for daily data
questions.oneLiner: Land the file, validate, transform, dedupe, load with idempotent writes, then check totals and alert.
simpleAnswer: Land the file, validate, transform, dedupe, load with idempotent writes, then check totals and alert.
ETL means Extract, Transform, Load. You pull data from a source, clean it, then save it where the app can use it.
A simple nightly job: the shop drops orders_YYYYMMDD.csv at 19:00. You must have clean rows in the database before 22:00.
Do not jump to Spark. Draw the stages first. Then pick the tool that fits the file size.

The usual design is to land the file with a checksum, validate schema, transform to one item-code and UTC dates, dedupe on order_id, MERGE into the warehouse so reruns do not double-count, then compare row counts and money totals. Bad rows go to a reject table, never silent delete.
Here is how the pieces fit together.
Extract: Copy from SFTP/S3. Store the original. Record size and checksum.
Validate: Header, types, required fields, file not truncated.
Transform: Dates to ISO, item codes upper-case, prices as decimals.
Load: Partition by date. Upsert on order_id.
Observe: Counts, duration, reject %, amount total vs control file.
Original file is never edited.
Idempotent load is mandatory.
Rejects are stored with reasons.
Watch-outs in real systems
If pandas.read_csv the whole file, then Out of memory. Missed SLA. Fix: Scan or chunk. Write parquet.
If Append on retry, then Yesterday's orders count twice. Fix: MERGE on order_id.
If Silent drop of bad rows, then Stock is quietly wrong. Fix: Dead-letter table + alert if reject % > 0.5%.
SLA clock on a dashboard.
One job_id per run.
Same code for backfill of 30 days.

questions.title: How would you validate and handle bad records?
questions.oneLiner: Fail the whole file if the file itself is broken. Quarantine bad rows if most of the file is fine. Never drop rows in silence.
simpleAnswer: Fail the whole file if the file itself is broken. Quarantine bad rows if most of the file is fine. Never drop rows in silence.
Validation is a set of rules: required fields, types, allowed values, ranges, and 'does this item code exist?'.
If the header is wrong or the checksum fails, stop. Do not load a truncated file.
If 1% of rows have a missing item code, load the rest and write the 1% to orders_reject with reason=BAD_ITEM.
I split file-level failures from row-level failures. File broken: stop. A few bad rows: quarantine with a reason code, load the rest, alert if the reject rate spikes.
Two levels: file vs row.
Every reject has a reason.
Optional fields must not block core fields.
Watch-outs in real systems
If Fail the whole 20 GB for missing comments, then Business has no data. Fix: Only core fields are blocking.
If Load bad qty as 0, then Stock looks sold out. Fix: Reject. Do not guess.
If No alert on reject spike, then You learn next week. Fix: Page if reject % > threshold.

questions.title: What is idempotency and why does it matter in pipelines?
questions.oneLiner: Idempotent means running the same job twice gives the same stored result. Nightly jobs fail. You must be able to rerun without double-counting.
simpleAnswer: Idempotent means running the same job twice gives the same stored result. Nightly jobs fail. You must be able to rerun without double-counting.
If your load is INSERT only, a retry adds the same 2 million orders again. Stock and sales explode.
Idempotent load uses a business key: order_id. MERGE: update if it exists, insert if it does not. Or delete that date partition and reload it.
The job key should include the file date and checksum so you know which file you processed.
This is a must-answer for ETL. If you miss it, they assume you have not owned a production job.
I make the load idempotent on order_id plus source date. A retry, a crash at 80%, or a replay tomorrow does not double-count. I store job_id and checksum so I can prove what ran.
Business key first.
Rerun is a feature, not an emergency.
Never 'append and hope'.
Watch-outs in real systems
If Only unique in memory, then Two jobs in parallel both insert. Fix: Database constraint + MERGE.
If Delete all orders then load, then A fail after delete leaves an empty shop. Fix: Replace one date partition, not the whole table.
If No unique key in the file, then You cannot MERGE. Fix: Build a key: date+item+customer+qty+price, and tell the sender to add order_id.

questions.title: How would you find mismatched records in Python and SQL?
questions.oneLiner: Match on a business key in SQL or pandas/Polars. Exact matches stay in SQL. Use Python only to inspect leftovers and to join files that are not in the database yet.
simpleAnswer: Match on a business key in SQL or pandas/Polars. Exact matches stay in SQL. Use Python only to inspect leftovers and to join files that are not in the database yet.
A mismatch is a row in file A with no twin in file B, or the same key with a different qty or price.
In SQL: FULL OUTER JOIN on order_id, then filter where one side is null or qty differs.
In Python: build a dict keyed by order_id, or a Polars join. Do not nested-loop 2 million rows in pure Python.

The usual design is to join on order_id. Missing in warehouse, missing on website, quantity breaks, and price breaks become four result sets. SQL for data already loaded. Polars join for two big files. The agent only reads the break table.
Matching is deterministic.
Do not ask the LLM to 'see if these look the same'.
Keep break types separate so ops can work the queue.
Watch-outs in real systems
If Match on item name only, then Blue T-shirt vs blue hoodie mix. Fix: Use item code.
If Nested Python loops, then Too slow on 2M rows. Fix: Join in SQL or Polars.
If Float compare for prices, then 12.00 vs 12.0000001 looks like a break. Fix: Compare as decimal cents.
Index the join keys.
Store break_type on the result table.

questions.title: How would you make an LLM application production-ready?
questions.oneLiner: Treat it like any API: timeouts, retries, limits, logs, tests, a kill switch, and a way to change the model without rewriting the app.
simpleAnswer: Treat it like any API: timeouts, retries, limits, logs, tests, a kill switch, and a way to change the model without rewriting the app.
A demo calls OpenAI from a notebook. Production has auth, rate limits, tracing, cost caps, fallback models, and human review for risky actions.
You also need evaluation: a small set of golden questions you run on every prompt change.
Never log full personal data. Never let the model write to the orders table in v1.
This is how they see if you can own the service, not only a prompt.

The usual design is to ship a small Python service with a model adapter, timeouts, retries with jitter, caching, tracing, token and latency metrics, JSON-schema outputs, and a golden-question eval in CI. Writes stay behind a human. I can switch Gemini to Claude by changing config.
Here is how the pieces fit together.
Edge: HTTPS, auth, per-user rate limit.
App: Use-case service, not 'one giant prompt'.
Model adapter: Provider is swappable.
Safety: Schema validation, allow-listed tools.
Observe: Trace id, tokens, latency, error rate, cost.
Adapter for the LLM vendor.
Fail closed on money and writes.
Eval in CI so prompt edits cannot silently break.
Watch-outs in real systems
If No timeout, then One hung call blocks workers. Fix: Timeout + extra worker budget.
If Retry on 400, then You pay for the same bad prompt. Fix: Retry only 429/5xx.
If No golden set, then A prompt tweak breaks stock answers. Fix: 20 questions run on every merge.
Dashboards for latency p95, error %, tokens, $.
Feature flag to disable tools.
Runbook: if provider is down, switch model.

questions.title: How would you prevent hallucinations?
questions.oneLiner: Ground answers in retrieved or queried facts, force JSON, check every number against tool output, and say 'I do not know' when data is missing.
simpleAnswer: Ground answers in retrieved or queried facts, force JSON, check every number against tool output, and say 'Do not know' when data is missing.
A hallucination is a fluent answer that is not true. In a shop bot, that is 'WH-12 has 400 shirts' when SQL returned 40.
You cannot fully stop an LLM from guessing. You can stop guesses from reaching the user: retrieve first, calculate in Python, validate, refuse.
Lower temperature helps a bit. Grounding and checks help a lot.

questions.title: RAG vs fine-tuning
questions.oneLiner: Use RAG when facts change or you must cite documents. Use fine-tuning when you need a stable style or a skill, not a living catalog.
simpleAnswer: Use RAG when facts change or you must cite documents. Use fine-tuning when you need a stable style or a skill, not a living catalog.
RAG = retrieve then generate. You search your files or database, then the model writes using those chunks.
Fine-tuning = change the model weights with examples. Good for tone, format, or a skill like extracting JSON from messy text.
Shop catalog prices change daily. That is RAG or SQL, not a weekly fine-tune.
Fine-tuning is expensive and goes stale. RAG is the default for company knowledge.
The usual design is to RAG (or SQL) for policies and changing facts. then fine-tune only for style or a narrow extraction skill. For a shop assistant Start with RAG plus tools, not a custom model.
Changing facts → retrieve.
Style/skill → maybe fine-tune.
Start with RAG. Fine-tune later if you have data.
Watch-outs in real systems
If Fine-tune the whole catalog, then Stale by Tuesday. Fix: Query the catalog API.
If RAG without chunking thought, then Wrong paragraph retrieved. Fix: Tune chunk size and metadata filters.
If No eval, then You cannot tell which is better. Fix: Same golden questions for both.

Cost: RAG adds retrieval latency; fine-tune adds train cost.

questions.title: Design an AI-powered daily reporting system
questions.oneLiner: Batch the numbers in a normal ETL job. Use the LLM only to write the narrative from those numbers. Humans approve before it goes to the shop manager.
simpleAnswer: Batch the numbers in a normal ETL job. Use the LLM only to write the narrative from those numbers. Humans approve before it goes to the shop manager.
A daily report should not let the model query raw 20 GB files. Overnight: aggregate sales, stock, and breaks into a small metrics table.
Morning: a job loads yesterday's metrics, asks the LLM for a short summary, validates every figure, stores draft + JSON, then a human clicks send.
If metrics are missing, do not invent a story.

The usual design is to compute metrics with ETL, then a small LangGraph job: load metrics → draft summary → validate numbers → human approve → email. The LLM never sees the raw file. If validation fails, the report is held.
Here is how the pieces fit together.
Metrics job: SQL aggregates: units, revenue, top items, break counts.
Writer job: LLM turns JSON into 8 bullets.
Guard: Every number in the draft must be in metrics JSON.
HITL: Manager approves in a queue.
Deliver: Email/Slack + store the exact prompt and output.
Numbers from ETL.
LLM is a writer, not an analyst of raw dumps.
Approval for anything that leaves the company.
Watch-outs in real systems
